papers.title: GPSNorm: Gaussian Process Spatial Normalization for Spatial Transcriptomics
papers.summary: GPSNorm is a computational method that uses Gaussian Process models to normalize spatial transcriptomics data, correcting for technical variation while preserving true spatial patterns in gene expression. This addresses a common problem where sequencing depth, batch effects, or tissue artifacts can distort readings across a tissue section. By modeling normalization as a spatially smooth process, it aims to make downstream analyses like clustering or differential expression more reliable.
papers.why: Accurate spatial normalization is essential for correctly interpreting spatial transcriptomics data from brain tissue, ensuring that observed gene expression patterns around interneurons or perineuronal nets reflect biology rather than technical noise.

papers.title: A deep learning representation and spatial Bayesian cell-type deconvolution for spatial transcriptomics.
papers.summary: This paper presents a computational method that combines a deep learning-based representation of spatial transcriptomics data with a spatial Bayesian model to deconvolve cell types within tissue spots. The approach aims to more accurately estimate the mixture of cell types present at each spatial location by leveraging both gene expression patterns and spatial context. This could improve resolution and accuracy when mapping cell-type composition across complex tissues like brain sections.
papers.why: Accurate cell-type deconvolution in spatial transcriptomics is essential for precisely mapping interneuron subtypes and their spatial relationship to perineuronal nets in brain tissue, directly supporting the spatial transcriptomics component of this PhD project.

papers.title: PGST: A Prototype-Guided Parameter-Efficient Network for Spatial Transcriptomics Prediction.
papers.summary: PGST is a computational method designed to predict spatial transcriptomics data from tissue images using a prototype-guided approach that requires fewer parameters than typical deep learning models. It likely uses representative 'prototype' patterns learned from training data to efficiently map histology image features to gene expression levels across tissue locations. This makes spatial transcriptomics prediction more computationally efficient, potentially enabling broader use on standard histology images without requiring full spatial sequencing.
papers.why: This method could help predict spatial gene expression from tissue images, offering a potentially efficient tool for analyzing spatial transcriptomics data in brain tissue relevant to studying mitophagy and autophagy gene programs in interneurons and their perineuronal net microenvironments.
papers.figure: The main architecture figure showing how prototype features are extracted and used to guide gene expression prediction from histology images.

papers.title: AddaGCN: Spatial transcriptomics deconvolution using graph convolutional networks with adversarial discriminative domain adaptation.
papers.summary: AddaGCN is a computational method that deconvolves spatial transcriptomics data to estimate the cell-type composition of each spatial spot. It combines graph convolutional networks, which capture spatial relationships between neighboring spots, with adversarial discriminative domain adaptation to transfer cell-type knowledge from single-cell reference data to spatial data despite differences between datasets. This approach aims to improve accuracy in mapping cell types onto tissue sections compared to existing deconvolution tools.
papers.why: Accurate deconvolution tools like this could help resolve cell-type composition, including interneuron subtypes, within spatial transcriptomics datasets of brain tissue relevant to this project.

papers.title: UNIPRO enables protein inference and panel expansion across single-cell and spatial transcriptomics
papers.summary: UNIPRO is a computational tool designed to infer protein expression levels from single-cell and spatial transcriptomics data. It works by expanding gene expression panels to predict corresponding protein abundance, effectively bridging the gap between RNA and protein measurements. This allows researchers to gain proteomic-level insights from existing transcriptomic datasets without needing additional experimental protein assays.
papers.why: This tool could help expand limited protein panels in spatial transcriptomics experiments to infer additional markers relevant to interneuron subtypes and perineuronal net components without requiring separate proteomic assays.

papers.title: Brazilin attenuates methylglyoxal‑induced endothelial injury by enhancing eIF5A hypusination and inhibiting the AMPK/mTOR‑mediated autophagy/apoptosis axis <i>in vitro</i> and <i>in vivo</i>.
papers.summary: This study investigates how brazilin, a natural compound, protects endothelial cells from damage caused by methylglyoxal, a toxic sugar byproduct. The researchers found that brazilin works by boosting a protein modification called eIF5A hypusination while blocking the AMPK/mTOR signaling pathway that normally triggers autophagy and cell death. These effects were confirmed in both cell culture experiments and animal models, suggesting brazilin could be a therapeutic candidate for vascular damage caused by metabolic stress.
papers.why: Although focused on endothelial cells rather than neurons, this paper's mechanistic insights into AMPK/mTOR-mediated autophagy regulation could inform parallel investigations of autophagy/mitophagy pathways in neuronal contexts within the PhD project.

papers.title: From synaptic development to degeneration: a narrative review of small molecule strategies targeting alpha-synuclein in Parkinson's disease.
papers.summary: This paper reviews small molecule strategies aimed at targeting alpha-synuclein, a protein central to Parkinson's disease pathology, tracing its role from normal synaptic development through to its contribution to neurodegeneration. It likely discusses how alpha-synuclein aggregation disrupts synaptic and cellular function, and surveys drug candidates designed to prevent or reverse this process. As a narrative review, it synthesizes existing literature rather than presenting new experimental data.
papers.why: Alpha-synuclein pathology intersects with autophagy and mitophagy dysfunction in neurons, which is directly relevant to understanding degeneration mechanisms in Parkinson's disease affecting brain circuitry.

papers.title: Molecular Mechanisms Underlying FCCP-Induced Mitophagyin Human Airway Smooth Muscle Cells.
papers.summary: This study investigates how the mitochondrial uncoupler FCCP triggers mitophagy, the selective clearance of damaged mitochondria, in human airway smooth muscle cells. The authors likely examine key molecular players such as PINK1/Parkin signaling and autophagy machinery to map out the pathway. Since airway smooth muscle cells are not neurons, the findings mainly inform general mitophagy biology rather than brain-specific mechanisms.
papers.why: The study could offer transferable insights into core mitophagy signaling pathways that may parallel mechanisms relevant to neuronal mitophagy, even though the cell type differs from the brain focus of this PhD project.
